people/anne-hutchinson/summary: Puritan laywoman whose meetings in Boston expounded John Cotton’s sermons and charged most Massachusetts ministers with preaching a "covenant of works". In the Free Grace (Antinomian) Controversy she was tried by the General Court (November 1637), banished, and excommunicated (March 1638); she settled in Rhode Island and was killed in New Netherland in 1643. Later celebrated as a pioneer of religious liberty and women’s religious leadership.
people/anne-hutchinson/keyIdeas/0: Assurance comes from the Spirit’s witness, not sanctification
people/johannes-cocceius/summary: Bremen-born Hebraist whose Summa doctrinae de foedere et testamento Dei (1648) gave classic shape to federal (covenant) theology, reading Scripture as the historical unfolding of covenants and the progressive "abrogation" of the covenant of works. His followers clashed with Gisbertus Voetius’ party, including over whether the fourth commandment binds Christians as a strict Sabbath.
people/johannes-cocceius/keyIdeas/0: Covenant of works and covenant of grace
people/thomas-boston/summary: Minister of Ettrick in the Scottish Borders, author of Human Nature in its Fourfold State (1720). He recommended The Marrow of Modern Divinity, whose republication (1718) and condemnation by the General Assembly (1720) produced the Marrow controversy over the free offer of the gospel and the relation of law and grace.
people/thomas-boston/keyIdeas/0: Free offer of Christ to all sinners
people/thomas-boston/keyIdeas/1: Repentance follows rather than qualifies for faith
people/rousas-rushdoony/summary: Armenian-American Calvinist whose Institutes of Biblical Law (1973) launched Christian Reconstructionism, arguing that the law of Moses, including its civil penalties, remains God’s standard for every society. He also championed Christian schooling and home-schooling. Critics across the Reformed world regarded his programme as a misreading of covenant history.
people/rousas-rushdoony/keyIdeas/0: Theonomy: God’s law for all spheres
people/rousas-rushdoony/keyIdeas/2: Christian education independent of the state
people/martin-chemnitz/summary: The "second Martin" of Lutheranism, author of the Examination of the Council of Trent (1565–73) and a principal drafter of the Formula of Concord (1577), which settled intra-Lutheran disputes including those over law and gospel and the third use of the law.
people/krister-stendahl/summary: Swedish biblical scholar whose essay "The Apostle Paul and the Introspective Conscience of the West" (1963) and Paul among Jews and Gentiles (1976) argued that Paul’s concern was the inclusion of Gentiles, not the troubled Western conscience, and that Romans 9–11 leaves Israel’s salvation to God. A pioneer of Jewish–Christian dialogue and of the "new perspective" on Paul.
people/krister-stendahl/keyIdeas/0: Paul as apostle to the Gentiles rather than convert from Judaism
people/krister-stendahl/keyIdeas/1: Romans 9–11 as the climax of Romans
people/joseph-rabinowitz/summary: Jewish lawyer from Bessarabia who, after a visit to Palestine in 1882, came to believe in Jesus as Messiah and founded in Kishinev the congregation "Israelites of the New Covenant" (1884), keeping Jewish customs such as circumcision and the Sabbath: a forerunner of modern Messianic Judaism.
people/joseph-rabinowitz/keyIdeas/0: Jesus as "our brother" and Messiah of Israel
people/darrell-bock/summary: American evangelical New Testament scholar who, with Craig Blaising, articulated "progressive dispensationalism" (1993): the Davidic kingdom is already inaugurated in Christ’s present reign, while a future for national Israel remains.
people/darrell-bock/keyIdeas/1: Israel and the Church distinct but not separate
people/douglas-moo/summary: American evangelical commentator on Romans and Galatians who argued, notably in Five Views on Law and Gospel (1993/1996), that the Mosaic law as a whole, including the Decalogue as such, belongs to the old era and that Christians are bound by "the law of Christ", a view close to New Covenant Theology.
people/stephen-wellum/summary: Canadian-born Baptist theologian who with Peter Gentry wrote Kingdom through Covenant (2012), proposing "progressive covenantalism": the biblical covenants unfold progressively and are all fulfilled in Christ, a middle way between covenant theology and dispensationalism that grounds believer’s baptism.
people/theophilus-of-antioch/summary: Late second-century bishop of Antioch whose apology To Autolycus contains the earliest explicit Christian argument that God created matter itself out of nothing, against the Platonist view that God merely shaped eternal matter. He is also the first known writer to call God a “triad”.
people/theophilus-of-antioch/keyIdeas/1: God’s power exceeds an artisan’s, who needs material
people/galileo-galilei/summary: Tuscan astronomer and physicist whose telescopic discoveries (1609–10) supported Copernican heliocentrism. In his Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615) he argued, drawing on Augustine, that Scripture accommodates its language to ordinary speech and does not teach astronomy. Admonished in 1616, he was tried by the Roman Inquisition after his Dialogue (1632), forced to abjure in 1633 and kept under house arrest until his death. He remained a professing Catholic.
people/galileo-galilei/keyIdeas/1: Scripture teaches how to go to heaven, not how the heavens go
people/galileo-galilei/keyIdeas/2: Two books: Scripture and nature cannot truly conflict
people/charles-darwin/summary: English naturalist whose On the Origin of Species (1859) argued that species arise by descent with modification through natural selection. Trained at Cambridge with a view to Anglican ordination and once an admirer of Paley, he moved gradually from orthodox belief to what he called agnosticism, partly through the problem of suffering (including the death of his daughter Annie, 1851). He is buried in Westminster Abbey.
people/charles-darwin/keyIdeas/2: Suffering in nature as a problem for design
people/gottfried-leibniz/summary: German Lutheran polymath who coined the word “theodicy” in his Essais de Théodicée (1710), arguing that God, being perfectly wise and good, chose to create the best of all possible worlds, in which permitted evils serve a greater harmony. He also worked for reunion between Catholics and Protestants.
people/thomas-chalmers/summary: Scottish evangelical minister, mathematician and leader of the 1843 Disruption that created the Free Church of Scotland. From about 1814 he popularised the “gap” (ruin-restoration) reading of Genesis 1:1-2, allowing the vast ages of the new geology to fall before the six days. He wrote a Bridgewater Treatise on natural theology (1833).
people/asa-gray/summary: Harvard botanist, Darwin’s chief American correspondent and a devout orthodox Protestant who argued that natural selection was compatible with design and providence: God could work through variation and selection. His essays were collected as Darwiniana (1876).
people/pierre-teilhard-de-chardin/summar: French Jesuit palaeontologist who worked for many years in China (including on Peking Man) and developed a sweeping evolutionary cosmology converging on an “Omega Point” identified with the cosmic Christ. Barred by his superiors from publishing theology in his lifetime, his Phenomenon of Man (1955) became widely influential; the Holy Office issued a monitum urging caution in 1962.
people/henry-m-morris/summary: American Baptist engineer who co-wrote The Genesis Flood (1961) with theologian John C. Whitcomb, reviving “flood geology” and launching modern young-earth creationism. He founded the Institute for Creation Research (1970), and the movement spread worldwide.
people/meredith-kline/summary: Reformed Old Testament scholar who, building on Arie Noordtzij (1924), developed the “framework” interpretation of Genesis 1 in “Because It Had Not Rained” (1958): the six days are a literary-theological structure (two triads of kingdoms and rulers), not a chronology.
people/francis-collins/roles/1: director of the Human Genome Project
people/francis-collins/summary: American geneticist who led the Human Genome Project and later the U.S. National Institutes of Health. An adult convert from atheism (influenced by C. S. Lewis), he argued in The Language of God (2006) for “BioLogos” — evolutionary creation — and founded the BioLogos Foundation in 2007.
people/francis-collins/keyIdeas/1: Common descent compatible with Christian faith
people/michael-behe/summary: American Catholic biochemist at Lehigh University whose Darwin’s Black Box (1996) argued that some molecular systems are “irreducibly complex” and best explained by intelligent design. He accepts common descent and an old earth; critics dispute irreducible complexity scientifically, and the Kitzmiller court (2005) heard his testimony.
people/john-hick/summary: English philosopher of religion (United Reformed Church) whose Evil and the God of Love (1966) contrasted “Augustinian” and “Irenaean” theodicies and developed the latter as “soul-making”. He later became known for religious pluralism.
people/john-hick/keyIdeas/3: Copernican revolution in theology of religions
people/john-k-roth/summary: American philosopher at Claremont McKenna College and Holocaust scholar whose essay “A Theodicy of Protest” (1981) argued that after Auschwitz faith must protest against God’s permission of waste and horror rather than justify it, while still hoping in God.
